knowledge_point.title: Transforming First-Order Linear ODEs Using Integrating Factors

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)$:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{11}{3}\right)\cdot y=\cos{\left(3 x \right)}$
Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x)) = I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{11}{3}$ and $Q(x)=\cos{\left(3 x \right)}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(\frac{11}{3}\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{11}{3}\right)\cdot y\right) & =I(x)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(3 x \right)}\right) \\ I(x)\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)I(x)y & =\left(e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(3 x \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\right)\right) & =\left(e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(3 x \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-5$ and $Q(x)=3{e}^{3x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -5\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-5x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-5x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y) & ={e}^{-5x}\cdot 3{e}^{3x} \\ {e}^{-5x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5{e}^{-5x}\cdot y & =3{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-5x}) & =3{e}^{-2x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-5x})\text{d}x & =\int 3{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-5x} & =-\frac{3{e}^{-2x}}{2}+C \\ y & =-\frac{3{e}^{3x}}{2}+C{e}^{5x}\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}y=\frac{2x}{5}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{5}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{2x}{5}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1/5\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x/5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{x/5}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/5}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}y) & ={e}^{x/5}\cdot \frac{2x}{5} \\ {e}^{x/5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}{e}^{x/5}\cdot y & =\frac{2x}{5}{e}^{x/5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/5}) & =\frac{2x}{5}{e}^{x/5} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/5})\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2x}{5}{e}^{x/5}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x) =$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x) =$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=1.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int 1\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+1y) & =e^{x}\cdot 1 \\ e^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{x}y & =e^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x}) & =e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int e^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{x} & =1\left(1 e^{x}\right)+C \\ ye^{x} & =e^{x}+C \\ y & =\left(C + e^{x}\right) e^{- x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(e^{(0)})+C}{(e^{(0)})} \\ 7 & =\frac{1+C}{1} \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=1 + 6 e^{- x}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $f_x(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\left(x + 2\right)^{y^{2}}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=x + 2\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=1\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}u^{y^{2}}&=\left(y^{2}\right)\,u^{y^{2} - 1}\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(u^{y^{2} - 1} y^{2}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)\\
&=y^{2} \left(x + 2\right)^{y^{2} - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for $x + 2>0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(0,- \frac{1}{2})&=\left(u_0^{3 \left(0\right)} \left(3 \left(0\right) + 1\right)\right)\cdot\left(2\right)\\
&=\left(1\right)\cdot\left(2\right)\\
&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{e^{- x y}}{x y - 2},
$$

the partial derivative with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{h(x,y)e^{- x y}}{\left(x y - 2\right)^2}.
$$

Find $h(x,y)$, where $x y - 2\ne0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $x$ constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Write $N=e^{- x y}$ and $D=x y - 2$. The component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{y}&=- x e^{- x y}, \\
D_{y}&=x.
\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule differentiates the exponent first; its inner derivative is $- x$. Apply the quotient rule, keeping its subtraction and squared denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=\frac{N_{y}D-ND_{y}}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{\left(- x e^{- x y}\right)D-N\left(x\right)}{D^2} \\
&=\frac{e^{- x y}\left(- x^{2} y + x\right)}{\left(x y - 2\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last step factors the common nonzero exponential $e^{- x y}$ from the numerator. Comparing with the supplied form gives $h(x,y)=- x^{2} y + x$. These expressions apply where $x y - 2\ne0$.

question.:question/problem: Find $f_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=x^{2} y- 3 y^{3} \cos{\left(x \right)}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as constant. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{2} y) &=y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{2}) \\
&=y\cdot \left(2 x\right) \\
&=2 x y\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(- 3 y^{3} \cos{\left(x \right)}) &=- 3 y^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\cos{\left(x \right)}) \\
&=- 3 y^{3}\cdot \left(- \sin{\left(x \right)}\right) \\
&=3 y^{3} \sin{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $f_{x}(x,y)=2 x y + 3 y^{3} \sin{\left(x \right)}$.

question.:question/problem: Find $f_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=x \ln{\left(y \right)}+y \ln{\left(x \right)}+e^{2 x + y}+\frac{x}{y}$, where $x>0$ and $y>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as constant. First write $e^{2 x + y}=e^{2 x}\cdot e^{y}$ to expose the held exponential factor. Write reciprocal powers as negative powers, using $\frac{1}{y^n}=y^{-n}$ for positive $n$. The logarithm of the held variable is a constant multiplier. Apply the sum and constant multiple rules term by term.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(x \ln{\left(y \right)}) &=x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\ln{\left(y \right)}) \\
&=x\cdot \left(\frac{1}{y}\right) \\
&=\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y \ln{\left(x \right)}) &=\ln{\left(x \right)}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\
&=\ln{\left(x \right)}\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=\ln{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{2 x + y}) &=e^{2 x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(e^{y}) \\
&=e^{2 x}\cdot \left(e^{y}\right) \\
&=e^{2 x + y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) &=x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) \\
&=x\cdot \left(- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\right) \\
&=- \frac{x}{y^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Combining the terms,

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{y}(x,y) &=\frac{x}{y}+\ln{\left(x \right)} \\ &\quad +e^{2 x + y}- \frac{x}{y^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\cos(x-y^{3})$, which limit of a difference quotient represents $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold $y$ constant. The definition gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}.
$$

Replace every occurrence of $x$ by $(x+h)$ in the function, preserving each operator and its input:

$$
f(x+h,y)=\cos((x+h)-y^{3}).
$$

Subtract the entire original function value and divide by $h$:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\left(\cos((x+h)-y^{3})-\cos(x-y^{3})\right)
$$

Only $x$ changes, and $h\ne 0$ before taking the limit.

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{4} \ln{(y )}-2 \sqrt{x} y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{4} \ln{(y )})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2 \sqrt{x} y) \\  & =\ln{(y )}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{4})-2 y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\ln{(y )}\cdot (4 x^{3})-2 y\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{x}}\right) \\  & =4 x^{3} \ln{(y )}-\frac{y}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,e)} & =4 (1)^{3} \ln{(e)}-\frac{(e)}{\sqrt{(1)}} \\  & =4 - e\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+x \cdot y=- x \cdot y^{2}.
$$

Use the substitution $z=y^{-1}$.

Work on an interval where $x>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=x\\ q(x)&=- x\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- x\right)z=x.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - x\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{2}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{2}}\,z\right)=x \cdot e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{2}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{2}}z=- e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{2}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\frac{x^{2}}{2}} - 1.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{1}{C \cdot e^{\frac{x^{2}}{2}} - 1}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 3 \cdot y=3 \cdot y^{2} \cdot e^{x}.
$$

Use the substitution $z=y^{-1}$.

Work on an interval where $x>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-3\\ q(x)&=3 \cdot e^{x}\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(3\right)z=- 3 \cdot e^{x}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int 3\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{3 \cdot x}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{3 \cdot x}\,z\right)=- 3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{3 \cdot x}z=- \frac{3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}}{4}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{- 3 \cdot x} - \frac{3 \cdot e^{x}}{4}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{4 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{4 \cdot C - 3 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-3\\ q(x)&=2 \cdot e^{x}\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(3\right)z=- 2 \cdot e^{x}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int 3\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{3 \cdot x}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{3 \cdot x}\,z\right)=- 2 \cdot e^{4 \cdot x}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{3 \cdot x}z=- \frac{e^{4 \cdot x}}{2}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{- 3 \cdot x} - \frac{e^{x}}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{2 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{2 \cdot C - e^{4 \cdot x}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: y=\frac{4 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{4 \cdot C + e^{4 \cdot x}}
y=\frac{3 \cdot e^{2 \cdot x}}{3 \cdot C - 2 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}
y=\frac{2 \cdot e^{3 \cdot x}}{2 \cdot C - e^{4 \cdot x}}

question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=1\\ q(x)&=- \left(x+6\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-2\right)z=2 \cdot \left(x+6\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -2\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}\,z\right)=2 \cdot \left(x+6\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}z=- \left(\left(x+6\right) + \frac{1}{2}\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)} - \left(x+6\right) - \frac{1}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{- \frac{2}{- 2 \cdot C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x+6\right)} + 2 \cdot \left(x+6\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.

question.:question/problem: Given that $8^{z}=13,$ find the value of $z$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking $\log_{8}$ of both sides of the equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
8^{z} &= 13 \\
\log_{8}\left(8^{z}\right) &= \log_{8}\left(13\right) \\
z &= \log_{8}\left(13\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and then solve for $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
z &= \frac{\log(13)}{\log(8)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
z\approx 1.233
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{\prime}+5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-5x}.
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

We see that the right-hand side is $-18{e}^{-2x},$ and ${e}^{-2x}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, so we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-2x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
{y}_{p}^{\prime}=-2\alpha {e}^{-2x}.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{\prime}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\alpha {e}^{-2x}+5\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =-18{e}^{-2x} \\ 3\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =-18{e}^{-2x} \\ \alpha  & =-6\end{aligned}

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-6{e}^{-2x}.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-5x}-6{e}^{-2x}.

Multiplying the derivative equation by $\mathrm{d}x$ and moving its right side to the left gives

question.:question/problem:

$$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a solution to a differential equation, it must satisfy the equation for all values of $x$ in an interval where the function is defined and the equation is valid.

With that in mind, let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Differentiating $f(x)=- \frac{1}{x^{5}},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f\prime(x)&=\left(- \frac{1}{x^{5}}\right)\prime \\ &=-(-5)x^{-6} \\ &=\frac{5}{x^{6}} \\ &\not\equiv \frac{4}{x^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Substituting $y=- \frac{1}{x^{5}}$ and $y\prime=\frac{5}{x^{6}}$ into the original equation gives an identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}y\prime &\overset{?}{=}- \frac{5 y}{x} \\ \frac{5}{x^{6}} &\overset{?}{=}\frac{-5\left(- \frac{1}{x^{5}}\right)}{x} \\ \frac{5}{x^{6}} &=\frac{5}{x^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, the function $y=- \frac{1}{x^{5}}$ is a solution to our differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: II. Substituting $y=f(x)$ and $y\prime=f\prime(x)$ into the differential equation gives a true statement.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
y'=y,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

The derivatives of the proposed functions are provided:

- For $y=3 e^{x}$, $y'=3 e^{x}$.
- For $y=e^{x}$, $y'=e^{x}$.

Substitute each function and its derivative into the equation. Which functions are solutions throughout the stated interval? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A function is a **solution** if its derivative equals the differential equation's right-hand side at every point of the stated interval. Differentiate each candidate and substitute it for $y$.

For $y=2 e^{x}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y'&=2 e^{x}\\\text{RHS}&=1\cdot \left(2 e^{x}\right)\\&=2 e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The two expressions agree throughout the interval, so this function **is a solution**.

For $y=3 e^{x}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y'&=3 e^{x}\\\text{RHS}&=1\cdot \left(3 e^{x}\right)\\&=3 e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The two expressions agree throughout the interval, so this function **is a solution**.

For $y=e^{x}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y'&=e^{x}\\\text{RHS}&=1\cdot \left(e^{x}\right)\\&=e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The two expressions agree throughout the interval, so this function **is a solution**.

Select the functions verified above; do not select **None of the above**.

knowledge_point.title: Identifying Solutions to First-Order Differential Equations

question.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
y'=\frac{4}{e^{y/2}},\qquad x>0.
$$

Which functions are solutions throughout the stated interval? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A function is a **solution** if its derivative equals the differential equation's right-hand side at every point of the stated interval. Differentiate each candidate and substitute it for $y$.

For $y=-\ln\left(2 x + 3\right)$:

The logarithm arguments are positive because $x>0$. Using the exponential and logarithm identities gives

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{\frac{-\ln\left(2 x + 3\right)}{2}}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 x + 3}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y'&=- \frac{2}{2 x + 3}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{4}{e^{\frac{-\ln\left(2 x + 3\right)}{2}}}\\&=4 \sqrt{2 x + 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1$, $y'=- \frac{2}{5}$ whereas $\text{RHS}=4 \sqrt{5}$. Thus they are not identical, so this function **is not a solution**.

For $y=2\ln\left(x + 3\right)$:

The logarithm arguments are positive because $x>0$. Using the exponential and logarithm identities gives

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{\frac{2\ln\left(x + 3\right)}{2}}&=x + 3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y'&=\frac{2}{x + 3}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{4}{e^{\frac{2\ln\left(x + 3\right)}{2}}}\\&=\frac{4}{x + 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1$, $y'=\frac{1}{2}$ whereas $\text{RHS}=1$. Thus they are not identical, so this function **is not a solution**.

For $y=\ln\left(\left(2 x + 3\right)^2\right)$:

The logarithm arguments are positive because $x>0$. Using the exponential and logarithm identities gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\left(2 x + 3\right)^2}&=2 x + 3\\e^{\frac{\ln\left(\left(2 x + 3\right)^2\right)}{2}}&=2 x + 3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y'&=\frac{8 x + 12}{\left(2 x + 3\right)^{2}}\\\text{RHS}&=\frac{4}{e^{\frac{\ln\left(\left(2 x + 3\right)^2\right)}{2}}}\\&=\frac{4}{2 x + 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The two expressions agree throughout the interval, so this function **is a solution**.

Select the functions verified above; do not select **None of the above**.

$$

The first derivative is squared, so the equation is not linear in the derivative.

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+(2x)\ln(xy)&=\cos(x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}&=\cos(x)-((2x)\ln(xy))\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following first-order linear differential equations are inhomogeneous?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear ODE is **homogeneous** if its standard form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ has $Q(x)=0$ for every $x$. It is **inhomogeneous** if $Q$ is not identically zero.

- First, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+8xy=0.
$$

This equation is already in standard form. Here $Q(x)=0$ is identically zero, so this equation is homogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+8xy=4{x}^{4}.
$$

This equation is already in standard form. Here $Q(x)=4{x}^{4}$ is not identically zero, so this equation is inhomogeneous. Its value at $x=0$ does not determine whether it is identically zero.

- Finally, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+8xy=-4y.
$$

We move the term involving $y$ to the left, keeping the independent forcing on the right:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+8xy & =-4y \\ {y}^{′}+8xy+4y & =0 \\ {y}^{′}+(8x+4)y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Here $Q(x)=0$ is identically zero, so this equation is homogeneous.

Select ${y}^{′}+8xy=4{x}^{4}$.

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

where $Q$ is not identical to zero.

- First, we consider the equation

$$
2{y}^{′}-3{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2}=y+{x}^{2}.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side and the terms involving only $x$ on the right side, then divide through by $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{′}-3{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2} & =y+{x}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{′}-3{x}^{2}y-y-3{x}^{2} & ={x}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{′}+(-3{x}^{2}-1)y & =4{x}^{2} \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{-3{x}^{2}-1}{2}y & =\frac{4{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=\frac{4{x}^{2}}{2}$, which is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
1{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{3}=-3y-{x}^{3}.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side and the terms involving only $x$ on the right side, then divide through by $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}1{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{3} & =-3y-{x}^{3} \\ 1{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y+3y+3{x}^{3} & =-{x}^{3} \\ 1{y}^{′}+(3{x}^{2}+3)y & =-4{x}^{3} \\ {y}^{′}+\frac{3{x}^{2}+3}{1}y & =\frac{-4{x}^{3}}{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=\frac{-4{x}^{3}}{1}$, which is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

$$
2{y}^{′}-3y+{x}^{3}=-y+{x}^{3}.
$$

$$

$$

The forcing function is $Q(x)=0$, which is identically zero. Therefore, this equation is homogeneous.

Select $2{y}^{′}-3{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2}=y+{x}^{2}$; $1{y}^{′}+3{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{3}=-3y-{x}^{3}$.

knowledge_point.title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $$
\int 9 x\operatorname{sin}(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $I=\int 9 x\operatorname{sin}(x)\,\text{d}x$. Use integration by parts.

$$
\int uv^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x=uv-\int vu^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

Choose the linear factor as $u$:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =9 x \\ u^{\prime} & =9 \\ v^{\prime} & =\operatorname{sin}(x) \\ v & =-\operatorname{cos}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}uv & =9 x\left(-\operatorname{cos}(x)\right) \\ \int vu^{\prime}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(-\operatorname{cos}(x)\right)9\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-9 x\operatorname{cos}(x)+9\int \operatorname{cos}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-9 x\operatorname{cos}(x)+9(\operatorname{sin}(x))+C \\  & =-9 x\operatorname{cos}(x)+9\operatorname{sin}(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\int xe^{6 x}\,\text{d}x=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int xe^{6 x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′} & =e^{6 x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{e^{6 x}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot e^{6 x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{e^{6 x}}{6}-\int \frac{e^{6 x}}{6}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int xe^{6 x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot xe^{6 x}-\frac{1}{6}\cdot \int e^{6 x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot xe^{6 x}-\frac{1}{36}\cdot e^{6 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the linear terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int xe^{6 x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\frac{x e^{6 x}}{6} - \frac{e^{6 x}}{36}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (4 x - 8)e^{- 2 x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =4 x - 8\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=4 \\ {v}^{′} & =e^{- 2 x}\, & ⟹\,v=- \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (4 x - 8)\cdot e^{- 2 x}\,\text{d}x & =(4 x - 8)\cdot \left(- \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}\right)-\int \left(- \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}\right)\cdot 4\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4 x - 8)e^{- 2 x}\,\text{d}x & =- \frac{1}{2}\cdot (4 x - 8)e^{- 2 x}+2\cdot \int e^{- 2 x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =- \frac{1}{2}\cdot (4 x - 8)e^{- 2 x}-e^{- 2 x}+C \\  & =-\frac{(4 x - 6)e^{- 2 x}}{2}+C \\  & =(3 - 2 x)e^{- 2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the linear terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4 x - 8)e^{- 2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\left(3 - 2 x\right)e^{- 2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$
